note: Plain-language summary for smallholder farmers. Every entry lists the sources it was written from. Reference material for the model and the farmer, not a diagnosis. Not yet reviewed by an agronomist or extension officer: please confirm before relying on it.

entries.name: Nitrogen deficiency
entries.signs: Plants pale yellow-green. Yellowing starts at the tip of older, lower leaves and runs along the midrib in a V shape; in bad cases lower leaves turn brown and die ("firing").
entries.distinguish: Starts on lower, older leaves (sulfur and zinc start on young leaves). The yellow follows the midrib; potassium yellows the leaf edges instead.
entries.checkInField: Compare lower and upper leaves of 10 plants; look for the V from the tip along the midrib; compare with a well-fertilized row; note when fertilizer or manure was last applied.
entries.byStage: Most likely during fast growth from knee-high, when the plant takes up most of its nitrogen.
entries.likelyWhen: After heavy rain or waterlogging (nitrogen is lost from wet, saturated soil); on sandy soils with little organic matter; when no top-dressing was given before the growth spurt.
entries.actNow: Top-dress nitrogen (fertilizer or well-rotted manure) while the crop is still growing fast, before tasselling; ask your extension officer how much for your soil.
entries.prevent: Split nitrogen: a small amount at planting and most of it just before the fast-growth stage. Add manure or compost; rotate with legumes.

entries.name: Potassium deficiency
entries.signs: Lower leaves yellow and then brown along the edges, starting at the tip; stalks weak and plants may fall over late in the season.
entries.distinguish: Burn on leaf edges of older leaves (nitrogen follows the midrib in a V).
entries.checkInField: Look at the edges of the lowest leaves on 10 plants; push a few stalks to test their strength.
entries.byStage: Older leaves first; weak stalks show near harvest.
entries.likelyWhen: Sandy soils (potassium washes out), and fields where stalks and residues are always removed.
entries.actNow: Ask your extension officer about potassium fertilizer; a soil test confirms it.
entries.prevent: Return crop residues or manure to the field; on sandy soils give potassium during the season, not all before planting.

sources.title: University of Nebraska CropWatch: Key to nutrient deficiencies of corn and sorghum

entries.name: Phosphorus deficiency
entries.signs: Young plants dark green with purple leaf tips and edges, starting on the lower leaves; growth slow.
entries.distinguish: Purple on young plants. Some varieties turn purple more than others, and the colour often fades before plants are waist-high.
entries.checkInField: Check young plants after a cold or wet spell; compare varieties and parts of the field.
entries.likelyWhen: Cool, wet weather followed by warm sun; compacted, very wet or very dry soil; acid soil (below pH 5.5 phosphorus is much less available).
entries.actNow: Little helps once seen; plants often recover as roots grow. Note the field for next season.
entries.prevent: Place phosphorus near the seed at planting, lime acid soils, and avoid compaction.

sources.title: University of Nebraska CropWatch: Key to nutrient deficiencies of corn and sorghum
Mississippi State University Extension: Corn fertilization (P3591)

entries.name: Sulfur deficiency
entries.signs: Whole young (upper) leaves turn evenly pale yellow, without dead patches; plants pale and stunted.
entries.distinguish: Young leaves first (nitrogen starts on old leaves). Evenly yellow; zinc gives white bands in the lower half of the leaf instead.
entries.checkInField: Compare the newest leaves with the oldest on 10 plants; look for even yellowing on top and green leaves below.
entries.actNow: Ask your extension officer about a sulfur-containing fertilizer or manure; a soil test confirms it before you buy.
entries.prevent: Test the soil every few years; add manure or compost.

sources.title: University of Nebraska CropWatch: Key to nutrient deficiencies of corn and sorghum
Mississippi State University Extension: Corn fertilization (P3591)

entries.name: Zinc deficiency
entries.signs: Young leaves have white to pale yellow bands in the lower half of the leaf, either side of the midrib, later turning pale brown or grey; plants pale and short.
entries.distinguish: Bands on young leaves (sulfur yellows the whole young leaf evenly; magnesium stripes old leaves).
entries.checkInField: Look at the youngest leaves for white bands near the base of the leaf.
entries.actNow: Ask your extension officer about zinc; a soil test confirms it before you buy.
entries.prevent: Soil test and add manure or compost.

sources.title: University of Nebraska CropWatch: Key to nutrient deficiencies of corn and sorghum

entries.name: Magnesium deficiency
entries.signs: Older leaves show yellow stripes between the veins, later turning rust-brown; plants yellow-green.
entries.distinguish: Stripes between veins on old leaves (zinc bands and sulfur yellowing are on young leaves).
entries.checkInField: Compare old and young leaves; look for stripes between veins on the lower leaves.
entries.likelyWhen: Acid soils, where magnesium is less available.
entries.actNow: Ask your extension officer; liming with dolomitic lime adds magnesium on acid soils.
entries.prevent: Soil test and correct acidity.

sources.title: University of Nebraska CropWatch: Key to nutrient deficiencies of corn and sorghum

entries.name: Acid soil
entries.signs: Patches of short, poorly growing plants with weak roots, often with signs of several deficiencies (purple, yellow) at once.
entries.distinguish: Whole patches grow badly even with fertilizer; a soil test shows low pH.
entries.checkInField: Get a soil test (every few years); compare roots of stunted and healthy plants.
entries.likelyWhen: Below about pH 5.5 maize starts to suffer: aluminium and manganese become toxic and phosphorus, nitrogen, potassium, sulfur and magnesium are harder for roots to take up. High rainfall and years of fertilizer make soil more acid.
entries.actNow: Ask your extension officer to interpret a soil test and advise lime.
entries.prevent: Lime before the season so it has time to work; the best pH for maize is about 6 to 7.

sources.title: Mississippi State University Extension: Corn fertilization (P3591)

entries.name: Waterlogging
entries.signs: Stunted, yellow plants in the low or poorly drained parts of the field after heavy rain; water stands for days.
entries.distinguish: Follows the lie of the land (low spots, not rows or random plants) and appears within days of heavy rain. Often followed by nitrogen yellowing because wet soil loses nitrogen.
entries.checkInField: Look for standing water or soggy soil after rain; dig up one yellow plant and one healthy one and compare roots.
entries.likelyWhen: Heavy or long rains on flat, low-lying, clay or compacted soils with poor drainage.
entries.actNow: Open shallow channels to let standing water off. Once the soil drains, top-dress nitrogen to replace what was lost.
entries.prevent: Plant on ridges or raised beds in low spots, keep drains open, and choose deep, well-drained land for maize.

entries.name: Drought / moisture stress
entries.signs: Leaves roll and look dull grey-green, especially in the afternoon; plants recover overnight if stress is mild.
entries.distinguish: Rolling that eases in the morning points to moisture stress. Worst on sandy or shallow soils and on ridges.
entries.checkInField: Check plants in the morning and afternoon; dig 15 cm and feel whether the soil is dry.
entries.byStage: Most damaging at tasselling and cob formation; a dry spell then cuts yield most.
entries.likelyWhen: Low or erratic rainfall and late planting into a short season.
entries.actNow: Mulch the soil and water at tasselling if you can. If the crop is drying at harvest, harvest promptly: leaving it in the field in drought raises aflatoxin risk.
entries.prevent: Plant within about two weeks of the first good rains, when the soil is wet to 30 cm. Use drought-tolerant or early varieties, and keep residues as mulch.

entries.name: Fall armyworm
entries.signs: Ragged holes and see-through 'windowpane' patches on leaves; wet sawdust-like droppings (frass) in the whorl; caterpillars inside. Severe attack kills the growing point (dead heart).
entries.distinguish: Caterpillar has a pale upside-down Y on its head and four dark dots in a square near the tail. Stalk borer makes small holes in straight rows and tunnels in the stem; cutworm cuts seedlings at the ground.
entries.checkInField: From the 2-3 leaf stage, 2-3 times a week: check 20 plants in each of 5 places across the field (100 plants). Count plants with fresh damage or frass in the whorl.
entries.byStage: Seedlings: windowpanes, small holes, dead heart. Whorl: ragged holes and frass. Tasselling and cobs: caterpillars bore into cobs and eat the grain.
entries.likelyWhen: Late-planted fields are hit hardest; it attacks every crop stage and can arrive in large numbers.
entries.actNow: Crush egg masses and caterpillars on each visit; put ash or soil into damaged whorls; keep weeding. If 10-15 of every 100 plants are freshly damaged, contact your AGRITEX/extension officer before spraying.
entries.prevent: Plant early with the effective rains. Push-pull (intercrop with desmodium, Brachiaria grass around the edge), timely weeding, and varieties with good husk cover help.

entries.name: Maize stalk borer
entries.signs: Small holes in straight rows across the youngest leaves; dead heart in young plants; tunnels with frass inside stems, which may break; older caterpillars bore into cobs.
entries.distinguish: Holes in neat rows and tunnels in the stem (fall armyworm leaves ragged holes and wet frass in the whorl).
entries.checkInField: Check the newest leaves on 20 plants for rows of small holes; split one damaged stem to look for tunnels and caterpillars.
entries.byStage: Seedlings and whorl: rows of holes, dead heart. Later: stem tunnels, broken stalks, cob damage; damaged cobs can grow mould (aflatoxin).
entries.likelyWhen: Numbers build up through the season; caterpillars survive the dry season inside old stalks and stubble.
entries.actNow: Pull out plants with dead heart. Keep the field weeded, and remove wild sorghum nearby.
entries.prevent: After harvest, slash and plough in or destroy old stalks (or burn their leaves if stalks are kept for fencing). Intercrop or rotate with cowpea, soybean or cassava; push-pull with Napier grass and desmodium. Act together with neighbours.

entries.name: Cutworm
entries.signs: Young seedlings cut off at or just below ground level; small holes in the first leaves.
entries.distinguish: Plants cut at the base, at night (fall armyworm feeds in the whorl).
entries.checkInField: Dig gently around cut seedlings, in the top few cm of soil, for a curled grey-brown caterpillar.
entries.likelyWhen: Fields with weeds or crop residue at planting, where caterpillars hide.
entries.actNow: Dig out and destroy the caterpillars near damaged plants; protect stems with a collar of paper or card; keep natural enemies (wasps, ants).
entries.prevent: Remove weeds at least two weeks before planting, and plough and harrow before planting.

sources.title: Infonet-Biovision: Maize (pests, diseases and crop husbandry)

entries.name: Termites
entries.signs: Plants wilt and fall over; roots and stems eaten from inside; soil tunnels running up stems and roots.
entries.distinguish: Soil tunnels on stems and roots, and damage worst in dry spells (stalk borer tunnels are inside the stem with frass).
entries.checkInField: Pull up a wilted plant and look for soil tunnels and white termites on roots and stem base.
entries.byStage: Mostly older plants, from about three months after planting.
entries.likelyWhen: Dry spells; fields cultivated for many years; old wood and residue left in the field; maize left standing after it is ready.
entries.actNow: Harvest on time and do not leave harvested maize in stooks or heaps where termites are a problem.
entries.prevent: Plough to break nests and runways, rotate crops, and remove rotting wood and residue.

sources.title: Infonet-Biovision: Maize (pests, diseases and crop husbandry)

entries.name: Storage pests (weevil and larger grain borer)
entries.signs: Larger grain borer: neat round holes in husks, cobs and grain, with lots of fine grain dust. Weevil: hollowed kernels with irregular holes; small brown beetles with a long snout.
entries.distinguish: Grain borer leaves round holes and fine dust and attacks cobs; weevils have a snout and attack loose grain too.
entries.checkInField: Every 1-2 weeks, sieve a sample of stored grain and look for beetles, holes and dust; smell for mustiness.
entries.byStage: After harvest, in store (weevils can start in the field).
entries.likelyWhen: Maize left in the field after it is ready, grain not dried enough, unshelled cobs, warm humid stores; grain-borer losses can reach about a third of the grain in 3-6 months.
entries.actNow: Sort out and use or sell infested grain first; shell and re-dry grain; clean out dust and damaged grain.
entries.prevent: Harvest on time; dry grain to about 12-13% (a kernel cracks when bitten); shell before storing; store in airtight or sealed containers in a clean, raised store; inspect regularly.

entries.name: Maize streak virus
entries.signs: Narrow, broken white-to-yellow streaks running along the leaves, starting as small pale spots at the base of the youngest leaves. Plants infected young are stunted and give small or no cobs.
entries.distinguish: Fine broken streaks along the veins on scattered plants, often near grass or field edges (zinc gives broad bands; nutrient problems affect whole areas evenly).
entries.checkInField: Look at the youngest leaves of 20 plants for fine broken streaks; note whether affected plants are near grass or the field edge.
entries.byStage: Worst when plants are infected young.
entries.likelyWhen: Spread by small leafhoppers that breed on wild grasses during the rains; late or staggered planting and fields next to grassland are hit hardest.
entries.actNow: There is no cure. Keep grass weeds down around the field.
entries.prevent: Plant early and at the same time as neighbours; use streak-tolerant varieties; keep about 10 m of bare ground from earlier maize; remove old cereal residue.

entries.name: Maize lethal necrosis (MLN)
entries.signs: Fine yellow specks or mottling on young leaves that join into stripes; leaves then die from the edges inward; dead heart; stunted plants with short internodes; husks dry early and cobs are small and poorly filled.
entries.distinguish: Many plants die from the leaf edges inward, with dead hearts and early-drying husks (streak gives fine streaks; drought rolls leaves that recover overnight).
entries.checkInField: Look for mottled young leaves, dead hearts and drying husks; count affected plants and note where they are.
entries.byStage: All stages; plants infected young are hit hardest and may die.
entries.likelyWhen: Caused by two viruses together, carried by insects (thrips, aphids, beetles), by seed from infected crops, and on tools and people moving between fields. Continuous maize keeps it going.
entries.actNow: Report suspected MLN to AGRITEX / the Ministry of Agriculture straight away: as of 2025 it had not been reported in southern Africa. Pull out and burn suspected plants; do not feed them to livestock; do not save seed; clean tools and do not walk from this field into others.
entries.prevent: Use certified disease-free seed; rotate with legumes; leave up to two months with no maize; remove weed and grass hosts.

sources.title: CIMMYT (Prasanna & Suresh, 2025): Maize lethal necrosis and its management

entries.name: Grey leaf spot
entries.signs: Long, narrow, rectangular tan-to-grey spots with straight edges, boxed in by the leaf veins; spots join and kill leaves.
entries.distinguish: Narrow rectangles limited by the veins (northern leaf blight gives wider cigar-shaped spots).
entries.checkInField: Look at the lower and middle leaves of 20 plants for rectangular grey spots between veins.
entries.likelyWhen: Long periods of high humidity and wet leaves.
entries.actNow: Note the field; losses can reach 30-50% in bad years. Ask your extension officer if it spreads fast before tasselling.
entries.prevent: Plant resistant varieties; rotate crops; bury or remove infected residue.

sources.title: Infonet-Biovision: Maize (pests, diseases and crop husbandry)

entries.name: Northern leaf blight
entries.signs: Small oval water-soaked spots that grow into long grey-green to tan cigar-shaped spots; dark velvety spores after rain or dew; badly hit leaves look dried out.
entries.distinguish: Long cigar-shaped spots (grey leaf spot is narrow and rectangular between veins). Dried leaves can look like drought.
entries.checkInField: Look at the lower leaves of 20 plants for cigar-shaped spots; note how many leaves are affected.
entries.likelyWhen: Heavy, frequent rain, very humid air and cool temperatures (about 20-25 C); warm dry weather slows it.
entries.actNow: Note the field and keep an eye on upper leaves; ask your extension officer if upper leaves are affected before tasselling.
entries.prevent: Plant tolerant or resistant varieties; rotate crops; plough in residue after harvest.

sources.title: Infonet-Biovision: Northern leaf blight

entries.name: Common rust
entries.signs: Small powdery cinnamon-brown pustules on both sides of the leaves, turning black as the crop matures.
entries.distinguish: Raised powdery pustules that leave brown dust on your finger (leaf spots and blights are flat).
entries.checkInField: Rub a pustule: rust leaves brown powder. Note how many leaves are covered.
entries.likelyWhen: Spores blow in on the wind; Oxalis (sorrel) weeds can carry it.
entries.actNow: Note the field; ask your extension officer if upper leaves are heavily covered before tasselling.
entries.prevent: Plant resistant varieties; plough residue deeply; control Oxalis weeds.

sources.title: Infonet-Biovision: Maize (pests, diseases and crop husbandry)

entries.name: Ear and cob rots
entries.signs: Pink to red mould on cobs and grain, often starting at the cob tip; rotten, light cobs.
entries.distinguish: Mould on the cob itself, often where insects or birds damaged it.
entries.checkInField: Peel back the husks of 20 cobs at harvest and count mouldy ones.
entries.byStage: Cobs, from grain filling to harvest.
entries.likelyWhen: Fungi enter through the silk and through holes made by borers, earworms and birds; leaving the crop in the field late raises the risk of toxins (aflatoxin).
entries.actNow: Do not eat or feed mouldy cobs to animals (they can carry toxins); sort them out at harvest; harvest on time and dry well.
entries.prevent: Control stalk borers and fall armyworm; plant varieties with good husk cover; harvest promptly.

sources.title: Infonet-Biovision: Maize (pests, diseases and crop husbandry)
Infonet-Biovision: Storage pests

entries.name: Smut (common and head smut)
entries.signs: Common smut: swollen galls on stems, leaves, tassels or cobs, covered by a whitish skin that bursts to release black powder. Head smut: the tassel or cob is replaced by a mass of black spores with threads inside.
entries.distinguish: Black powdery galls; head smut has stringy threads among the spores.
entries.checkInField: Count plants with galls or smutted tassels and cobs.
entries.byStage: Mostly at tasselling and cob formation.
entries.likelyWhen: Head smut is carried on seed; spores stay in the soil.
entries.actNow: Cut off galls and smutted heads before they burst, and burn or bury them away from the field.
entries.prevent: Use clean certified seed and resistant varieties; rotate crops; remove volunteer maize.

sources.title: Infonet-Biovision: Maize (pests, diseases and crop husbandry)

entries.name: Striga (witchweed)
entries.signs: Small plants with pink-purple flowers growing from the roots of maize; the maize is stunted, yellowish and wilts even when the soil is moist. Damage starts before the weed comes up.
entries.distinguish: Look for the purple-flowered weed at the base of affected maize.
entries.checkInField: Count Striga plants around 20 maize plants; dig gently to see them attached to maize roots.
entries.byStage: Damage from early growth; the weed flowers mid-season.
entries.likelyWhen: Poor soils low in nitrogen, drier areas, and fields cropped with maize year after year.
entries.actNow: Pull Striga out before it flowers and sets seed, and keep weeding.
entries.prevent: Intercrop with desmodium (push-pull); rotate with trap crops such as sunflower, pulses or cotton; use Striga-tolerant varieties; improve soil fertility; keep it up for several years.
